title: Dumpling and the Chain
part: PART ONE: THE SHOP AT THE END OF INK LANE

pages.text:
*The Fourth Rule of Mapmaking: Pack less than you fear you'll need, and more than you hope you will.*

The trunk at the back of the shop had not seen the light of day in three years. It opened with a groan. It sounded exactly like a bear clearing its throat before demanding breakfast. Inside lay the dust of the past, and the tools of the present.

Master Finch lifted a folding table wrapped in oiled cloth. She unwrapped it with the slow precision of a surgeon. Then came the measuring chain. It was heavy. It was cold. Tam held it up. It clinked and jangled, a small, noisy orchestra of brass links that seemed to have strong opinions about being touched.

"Good," said Finch. "It needs to be heavy. A light chain lies."

In the yard outside, Dumpling the mule was chewing a piece of hay. He had the distinct air of a person who had been asked to do a favor and had decided to do it very slowly. He turned one large, dark eye toward the window. Then he looked back at his hay. It made it perfectly clear that he had heard nothing about leaving.
pages.image: Tam holds up a heavy brass measuring chain that clinks noisily, while an old grey mule chews hay outside the shop window with a stubborn, unimpressed expression.

pages.text:
Sixpence sat on the sill, ruffling her grey feathers and fixing Tam with a look that suggested she was already planning her escape.

"Strict instructions," Finch said, tapping the wicker basket she had set on the table. "You carry a note. You fly home. You do not nap in the treetops. Do you understand?"

Sixpence cooed, a low, rumbling sound that vibrated in the air.

Finch reached into her coat pocket and pulled out a small, shiny apple. She dangled it in front of Dumpling’s nose. The mule’s ears pricked forward. He stopped chewing. He looked at the apple, then at Finch, then at the apple again.

"One does not go into the wild without apples," Finch said, her voice dry as old parchment. "For the mule. And for morale."
pages.image: Master Finch dangles a shiny red apple in front of a grey mule's nose, while a grey pigeon with a white chest patch watches from a nearby wicker basket.

pages.text:
The ferry landing was a sucking mess of mud that smelled strongly of low tide and old salt. A boy stood there, tall and gangly, his red hair sticking up in three distinct directions that defied any known law of nature. He wore a coat too large for his frame and boots that were far too wet for the day, suggesting he had spent the morning walking through the river and then simply gave up trying to dry off.

His grin was so wide and gap-toothed that Tam suspected his jaw might have been a separate piece of machinery.

"Odd," Finch said, not bothering to introduce him as if the name were a brand of cheese. "This is Tam. She draws the lines. You know the rivers."

Odd extended both hands at once, shaking Tam’s right and left simultaneously.

"Heard you’re the one who blots," he said, laughing at a cloud that was passing overhead. "That’s a good thing. Means you’re trying. I’m Odd. I know where the water goes. Mostly."
pages.image: A tall, gangly boy with red hair and a wide gap-toothed grin shakes hands with a sturdy girl in a patched coat at a muddy river landing, both looking cheerful and slightly disheveled.

pages.text:
The road out of Verrin was a churn of mud and ambition. Academy apprentices filed past in neat rows, their horses polished until the coats reflected the sky like a puddle on a sunny day. Trumpets blared a tune that made Tam’s teeth ache.

Lucan Ravel sat in the window of a carriage lacquered green. It gleamed. He looked like a beetle’s shell that had decided to go to school. His fair hair was perfect. A gold compass swung gently against his chest, ticking with every bump in the road.

He paused. His eyes dropped to Tam’s small cart, the mule, and the pigeon in the basket. He raised his hand to his forehead. A mock salute. His expression was one of polite, exaggerated pity, the kind a cat gives a mouse that has just fallen off the table.

Tam felt heat rise in her cheeks. She did not look away. She looked at the green paint. Then at her own dusty wheels. Something settled in her stomach. Heavy. Cold.
pages.image: A boy in a green coat sits in the window of a polished green carriage, looking down with a mocking salute at a sturdy girl standing beside a small, dusty wooden cart.

pages.text:
The city walls slid past, the stone gray and indifferent. The last chimney smoke of Verrin fell behind them, a thin ribbon dissolving into the morning air.

Ahead lay a land of green and grey, vast and unmarked. No roads. No signs. Just the blank promise of the Uncharted Marches.

Tam’s stomach gave a lurch that had nothing to do with hunger. She pulled the small, stitched notebook from her satchel. The pages were thin, filled with crooked rivers and honest mistakes.

Finch, jolting gently beside her on the cart, did not speak. She merely reached over and tapped the cover of the book once, a soft, firm knock.

"Well," said Tam, closing the book and gripping the cart’s edge. "There’s the promise. Let’s see if we can keep it."
pages.image: A sturdy girl with a black braid holds a small stitched notebook, looking out at a vast, unmarked landscape of green hills and grey sky from the back of a moving wooden cart.
